answer.label: Not Ernest Hemingway — origin unknown
answer.authorDates: No documented source · possibly an anonymous 2000 Usenet post
answer.sourceLine: No source for this sentence has been found anywhere in Ernest Hemingway’s novels, short stories, poems or published letters. Wikiquote files it under “Disputed,” noting only that it “may have originated in a 2000 post to the Usenet group alt.support.depression,” and Check Your Fact rated the Hemingway attribution False in 2019 after two of his biographers rejected it — one of them on the grounds that the closing “you know?” is simply not how Hemingway wrote.

source.excerpt: I love sleep. My life has the tendency to fall apart when I’m awake, you know?
trail: Wikiquote ↗ lists the line in its Disputed section, not among his sourced quotations, with the note: “No source in Hemingway’s works has been found. May have originated in a 2000 post to the Usenet group alt.support.depression.”

Check Your Fact ↗ published a fact check on this exact sentence on 22 July 2019. Verdict: False. Searches of collections of Hemingway’s novels, poems and short stories failed to return any matching or similar phrase.

Two biographers were asked directly and both said no. Dearborn: “It’s definitely not Hemingway. This is the first time I’ve heard the quote.” Hutchisson: “Most likely not by Hemingway.” Archived text of the fact check ↗.

The pattern is well documented for this author generally: The Hemingway Society ↗ keeps a standing page on quotes he did not say, and names Goodreads, BrainyQuote, Quotefancy, iHeartIntelligence and Pinterest as the sites that keep them in circulation.
source.excerptNote: There is no fuller context to show. The line has never been located inside a novel, story, letter, interview or transcript — it circulates only as a free-floating sentence with a famous name attached.
source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted for this wording. Because the sentence has never been tied to any published work, there is no first-publication date to reason from — so it must not be treated as public domain. If Wikiquote’s lead is right and it began as a 2000 Usenet post, the words would belong to an unidentified modern author and would be in copyright.

author.name: Ernest Hemingway
author.heading: The man it gets pinned on
author.bio: Ernest Hemingway won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1954 for a body of work built on short declarative sentences and things left unsaid — a style so recognisable that it has become an open invitation to forgery. He is one of the internet’s most reliable magnets for unsourced aphorisms: The Hemingway Society ↗ maintains a page precisely because so many lines circulating under his name cannot be traced to him, and points at Goodreads, BrainyQuote, Quotefancy and Pinterest as the machinery that keeps them moving. This sleep line is one of those.

misattribution.heading: How a sourceless line became a Hemingway line
misattribution.intro: Nobody has ever produced a page, a letter or a transcript. What exists is a sentence, a famous name welded to it, and roughly two decades of copying.

items.why: Every large quote site runs it under his name with no work cited. Wikiquote ↗ puts it in its Disputed section and states plainly that no source in Hemingway’s works has been found.

Mary V. Dearborn, author of Ernest Hemingway: A Biography, told the Daily Caller News Foundation the syntax and diction are wrong — “Hemingway would never make an observation and then end it with ‘you know?’” James Hutchisson answered the same query with “Most likely not by Hemingway.” Both replies are quoted in full ↗.

The Goodreads entry ↗ carries no book, no page and no date — just “― Ernest Hemingway” and more than 9,500 likes. The Hemingway Society names exactly this class of site as the reason fake Hemingway quotes keep multiplying.

Wikiquote suggests the line “may have originated in a 2000 post to the Usenet group alt.support.depression” and cites a Google Groups message. Google has since retired public browsing of its Usenet archive, so that message can no longer be read; the lead is neither confirmed nor ruled out.

misattribution.truthLine: On the current record the honest answer is that nobody knows who wrote it — only that the evidence for Hemingway is nil ↗.

context.heading: A line that sounds like him, and isn’t
lead: It reads like late-night Hemingway — short, flat, faintly rueful, the self-knowledge of a man who has stopped arguing with himself. That resemblance is exactly why it travels. But when Check Your Fact ↗ went looking in 2019, searches of collections of his novels, poems and short stories returned no matching or similar phrase, and the verdict came back False.

The two biographers consulted were blunter than the search results. “It’s definitely not Hemingway. This is the first time I’ve heard the quote,” Mary V. Dearborn told the Daily Caller News Foundation; James Hutchisson answered, “Most likely not by Hemingway.” Dearborn also noted what is true of the real man: like many ‘sensitive’ types he had trouble with insomnia. Hemingway does discuss sleep in his personal letters — usually in the context of not getting any, telling F. Scott Fitzgerald about it in one and describing sleeping pills in another. Loving sleep was not his problem.
detailsBody: Wikiquote’s only lead is a citation to a thread in the Usenet group alt.support.depression, dated 2000. That citation points at Google Groups, which retired public browsing of its Usenet archive; the linked message no longer resolves to readable text, and the older raw-message endpoint returns a 404. So the suggestion cannot currently be confirmed or ruled out from the primary record, and Wikiquote itself only says the line may have originated there.

Quote Investigator ↗, the usual court of last resort for this kind of question, has no article on the phrase — a site search for the distinctive words returns nothing. That absence is not evidence of authenticity; it simply means no one has yet found an earlier printed appearance to trace.
